data.scenario_text: The function L(x)=8\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)\right]+25 models the water level, in feet, of a reservoir, where x=1 represents January, x=2 represents February, and so on.
data.part_a: What is the average water level of the reservoir?
data.part_b: What are the highest and lowest water levels of the reservoir?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the water level in November. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=25, so the reservoir averages \boxed{25\text{ ft}}.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=8, so the quantity rises 8 above the average value and falls 8 below it:

\text{maximum}=25+8=33\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=25-8=17\text{ ft}

The reservoir is highest in June at 33\text{ ft} and lowest in December at 17\text{ ft}, so the range of levels is \boxed{[17\text{ ft},\ 33\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the level follows a yearly cycle and repeats every 12 months.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} months, and so the pattern is shifted 3 months to the right: the level is at its average and rising in March, peaks in June, and is lowest in December.

Part (e). Substitute x=11 (November):

L(11)=8\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(11-3)\right]+25=8\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)+25

=8\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+25=-\frac{8\sqrt{3}}{2}+25

So the model gives approximately \boxed{18.1\text{ ft}} in November.

data.scenario_text: The function f(x)=16\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)\right]+63 models the average monthly temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, for a particular city, where x=1 represents January, x=2 represents February, and so on.

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid f(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=63, so the average temperature is \boxed{63^\circ\text{F}}.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=16, so the quantity rises 16 above the average value and falls 16 below it:

\text{maximum}=63+16=79^\circ\text{F}\qquad\text{minimum}=63-16=47^\circ\text{F}

The warmest month on average is August and the coolest is February, so the range of monthly average temperatures is \boxed{[47^\circ\text{F},\ 79^\circ\text{F}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the temperature pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} months, and so the sine pattern is shifted 5 months to the right: the temperature is at its average and rising in May, not in January. Equivalently, the warmest month is August and the coolest is February.

Part (e). Substitute x=7 (July):

Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=36, so the rider averages \boxed{36\text{ ft}} above the ground.

\text{maximum}=36+24=60\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=36-24=12\text{ ft}

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the water averages \boxed{12\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ ft}

High tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 16\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 8\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[8\text{ ft},\ 16\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 2 hours to the right: at 2:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 5:00 a.m. and again at 5:00 p.m.; low tide is at 11:00 a.m. and again at 11:00 p.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=12 (noon):

d(12)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(12-2)\right]+12=4\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{3}\right)+12

=4\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+12=-\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{2}+12

So the model gives approximately \boxed{8.5\text{ ft}} at noon.

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=14, so the water averages \boxed{14\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=14+4=18\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=14-4=10\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 18\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 10\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[10\text{ ft},\ 18\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 5 hours to the right: at 5:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 8:00 a.m. and again at 8:00 p.m.; low tide is at 2:00 p.m. and again at 2:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=7 (7:00 a.m.):

d(7)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(7-5)\right]+14=4\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{3}\right)+14

=4\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+14=\frac{4\sqrt{3}}{2}+14

So the model gives approximately \boxed{17.5\text{ ft}} at 7:00 a.m..

data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 3:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=10, so the water averages \boxed{10\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=6, so the quantity rises 6 above the average value and falls 6 below it:

\text{maximum}=10+6=16\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=10-6=4\text{ ft}

High tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 16\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 4\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[4\text{ ft},\ 16\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 2 hours to the right: at 2:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 5:00 a.m. and again at 5:00 p.m.; low tide is at 11:00 a.m. and again at 11:00 p.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=3 (3:00 a.m.):

d(3)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(3-2)\right]+10=6\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+10

=6\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+10=13

So the model gives exactly \boxed{13.0\text{ ft}} at 3:00 a.m..

data.scenario_text: The function H(t)=16\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(t-1)\right]+42 models a rider's height, in feet, above the ground on a Ferris wheel, where t is the number of minutes after the ride starts.
data.part_a: What is the rider's average height above the ground during one full revolution?
data.part_b: What are the rider's greatest and least heights above the ground?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the rider's height at 11 minutes after the ride starts. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=42, so the rider averages \boxed{42\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=16, so the quantity rises 16 above the average value and falls 16 below it:

\text{maximum}=42+16=58\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=42-16=26\text{ ft}

The rider reaches a maximum of 58\text{ ft} at 4 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 26\text{ ft} at 10 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[26\text{ ft},\ 58\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} minutes, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of t that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-1)=0 \implies t-1=0 \implies t=1

The phase shift is \boxed{1} minutes, and so the ride is shifted 1 minutes: the rider is at the height of the center and rising at 1 minutes after the ride starts, reaches the top at 4 minutes after the ride starts, and is lowest at 10 minutes after the ride starts.

Part (e). Substitute t=11 (at 11 minutes after the ride starts):

H(11)=16\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(11-1)\right]+42=16\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{3}\right)+42

=16\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+42=-\frac{16\sqrt{3}}{2}+42

So the model gives approximately \boxed{28.1\text{ ft}} at 11 minutes after the ride starts.

data.part_b: What are the highest and lowest water levels of the reservoir?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the water level in December. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=29, so the reservoir averages \boxed{29\text{ ft}}.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=8, so the quantity rises 8 above the average value and falls 8 below it:

\text{maximum}=29+8=37\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=29-8=21\text{ ft}

The reservoir is highest in May at 37\text{ ft} and lowest in November at 21\text{ ft}, so the range of levels is \boxed{[21\text{ ft},\ 37\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the level follows a yearly cycle and repeats every 12 months.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} months, and so the pattern is shifted 2 months to the right: the level is at its average and rising in February, peaks in May, and is lowest in November.

Part (e). Substitute x=12 (December):

L(12)=8\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(12-2)\right]+29=8\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{3}\right)+29

=8\left(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+29=-\frac{8\sqrt{3}}{2}+29

So the model gives approximately \boxed{22.1\text{ ft}} in December.

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=9, so the water averages \boxed{9\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=6, so the quantity rises 6 above the average value and falls 6 below it:

\text{maximum}=9+6=15\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=9-6=3\text{ ft}

High tide is at 5:00 a.m., when the depth is 15\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 11:00 a.m., when the depth is 3\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[3\text{ ft},\ 15\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

d(6)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(6-2)\right]+9=6\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)+9

Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=30, so the rider averages \boxed{30\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=24, so the quantity rises 24 above the average value and falls 24 below it:

\text{maximum}=30+24=54\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=30-24=6\text{ ft}

The rider reaches a maximum of 54\text{ ft} at 4 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 6\text{ ft} at 10 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[6\text{ ft},\ 54\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} minutes, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of t that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-1)=0 \implies t-1=0 \implies t=1

The phase shift is \boxed{1} minutes, and so the ride is shifted 1 minutes: the rider is at the height of the center and rising at 1 minutes after the ride starts, reaches the top at 4 minutes after the ride starts, and is lowest at 10 minutes after the ride starts.

Part (e). Substitute t=6 (at 6 minutes after the ride starts):

H(6)=24\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(6-1)\right]+30=24\sin\left(\frac{5\pi}{6}\right)+30

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=31, so the rider averages \boxed{31\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=18, so the quantity rises 18 above the average value and falls 18 below it:

\text{maximum}=31+18=49\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=31-18=13\text{ ft}

The rider reaches a maximum of 49\text{ ft} at 6 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 13\text{ ft} at 12 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[13\text{ ft},\ 49\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} minutes, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of t that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-3)=0 \implies t-3=0 \implies t=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} minutes, and so the ride is shifted 3 minutes: the rider is at the height of the center and rising at 3 minutes after the ride starts, reaches the top at 6 minutes after the ride starts, and is lowest at 12 minutes after the ride starts.

Part (e). Substitute t=7 (at 7 minutes after the ride starts):

H(7)=18\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(7-3)\right]+31=18\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)+31

=18\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)+31=\frac{18\sqrt{3}}{2}+31

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-4)=0 \implies x-4=0 \implies x=4

data.part_b: What is the range of the household's monthly electricity use?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the household's electricity use in September. Round to the nearest kilowatt-hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=827, so the household averages \boxed{827\text{ kWh}} per month.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=146, so the quantity rises 146 above the average value and falls 146 below it:

\text{maximum}=827+146=973\text{ kWh}\qquad\text{minimum}=827-146=681\text{ kWh}

The heaviest use is in May at 973\text{ kWh} and the lightest is in November at 681\text{ kWh}, so the range of monthly use is \boxed{[681\text{ kWh},\ 973\text{ kWh}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so use follows a yearly cycle and repeats every 12 months.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-2)=0 \implies x-2=0 \implies x=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} months, and so the pattern is shifted 2 months to the right: use is at its average and rising in February, peaks in May, and bottoms out in November.

Part (e). Substitute x=9 (September):

E(9)=146\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(9-2)\right]+827=146\sin\left(\frac{7\pi}{6}\right)+827

=146\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+827=754

So the model gives exactly \boxed{754\text{ kWh}} in September.

data.scenario_text: The function d(x)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)\right]+9 models the depth of the water, in feet, at a harbor, where x=0 represents midnight and x is the number of hours after midnight.

data.part_b: What are the greatest and least depths of the water at this harbor?
data.part_c: What is the period of this function? How many times does high tide occur in a day?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the depth of the water at 10:00 a.m.. Round to the nearest tenth of a foot.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=9, so the water averages \boxed{9\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=6, so the quantity rises 6 above the average value and falls 6 below it:

\text{maximum}=9+6=15\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=9-6=3\text{ ft}

High tide is at 6:00 a.m., when the depth is 15\text{ ft}, and low tide is at noon, when the depth is 3\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[3\text{ ft},\ 15\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 3 hours to the right: at 3:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 6:00 a.m. and again at 6:00 p.m.; low tide is at noon and again at midnight.

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (10:00 a.m.):

d(10)=6\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-3)\right]+9=6\sin\left(\frac{7\pi}{6}\right)+9

=6\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+9=6

So the model gives exactly \boxed{6.0\text{ ft}} at 10:00 a.m..

data.scenario_text: The function H(t)=18\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(t-1)\right]+33 models a rider's height, in feet, above the ground on a Ferris wheel, where t is the number of minutes after the ride starts.

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=33, so the rider averages \boxed{33\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=18, so the quantity rises 18 above the average value and falls 18 below it:

\text{maximum}=33+18=51\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=33-18=15\text{ ft}

The rider reaches a maximum of 51\text{ ft} at 4 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 15\text{ ft} at 10 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[15\text{ ft},\ 51\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} minutes, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-1)=0 \implies t-1=0 \implies t=1

H(2)=18\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(2-1)\right]+33=18\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+33

data.part_c: What is the period of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_d: What is the phase shift of this function, and what does it mean in this context?
data.part_e: Use the model to estimate the number of hours of daylight in October. Round to the nearest tenth of an hour.
data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=12, so the city averages \boxed{12\text{ hr}} of daylight.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=12+4=16\text{ hr}\qquad\text{minimum}=12-4=8\text{ hr}

The longest day is in December, with 16\text{ hr} of daylight, and the shortest is in June, with 8\text{ hr}, so the range is \boxed{[8\text{ hr},\ 16\text{ hr}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the daylight pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-9)=0 \implies x-9=0 \implies x=9

The phase shift is \boxed{9} months, and so the pattern is shifted 9 months to the right: daylight is at its average and increasing in September, which is an equinox. The longest day falls in December and the shortest in June, as expected in the Southern Hemisphere.

Part (e). Substitute x=10 (October):

L(10)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(10-9)\right]+12=4\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+12

=4\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+12=14

So the model gives exactly \boxed{14.0\text{ hr}} of daylight in October.

\text{maximum}=14+4=18\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=14-4=10\text{ ft}

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

d(11)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(11-3)\right]+14=4\sin\left(\frac{4\pi}{3}\right)+14

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=34, so the rider averages \boxed{34\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=16, so the quantity rises 16 above the average value and falls 16 below it:

\text{maximum}=34+16=50\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=34-16=18\text{ ft}

The rider reaches a maximum of 50\text{ ft} at 5 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 18\text{ ft} at 11 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[18\text{ ft},\ 50\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} minutes, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of t that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-2)=0 \implies t-2=0 \implies t=2

The phase shift is \boxed{2} minutes, and so the ride is shifted 2 minutes: the rider is at the height of the center and rising at 2 minutes after the ride starts, reaches the top at 5 minutes after the ride starts, and is lowest at 11 minutes after the ride starts.

Part (e). Substitute t=3 (at 3 minutes after the ride starts):

H(3)=16\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(3-2)\right]+34=16\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{6}\right)+34

=16\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)+34=42

So the model gives exactly \boxed{42.0\text{ ft}} at 3 minutes after the ride starts.

The warmest month on average is June and the coolest is December, so the range of monthly average temperatures is \boxed{[38^\circ\text{F},\ 66^\circ\text{F}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the temperature pattern repeats every 12 months, that is, once each year.

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} months, and so the sine pattern is shifted 3 months to the right: the temperature is at its average and rising in March, not in January. Equivalently, the warmest month is June and the coolest is December.

f(7)=14\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(7-3)\right]+52=14\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{3}\right)+52

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

data.solution_steps:
Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=29, so the reservoir averages \boxed{29\text{ ft}}.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=29+4=33\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=29-4=25\text{ ft}

The reservoir is highest in June at 33\text{ ft} and lowest in December at 25\text{ ft}, so the range of levels is \boxed{[25\text{ ft},\ 33\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} months, and so the level follows a yearly cycle and repeats every 12 months.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-3)=0 \implies x-3=0 \implies x=3

The phase shift is \boxed{3} months, and so the pattern is shifted 3 months to the right: the level is at its average and rising in March, peaks in June, and is lowest in December.

Part (a). The midline y=D is the average value of the oscillation, and for a rider on a wheel that is the height of the wheel's center, because the rider spends equal time above and below it. Here D=39, so the rider averages \boxed{39\text{ ft}} above the ground.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=16, so the quantity rises 16 above the average value and falls 16 below it:

\text{maximum}=39+16=55\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=39-16=23\text{ ft}

The rider reaches a maximum of 55\text{ ft} at 4 minutes after the ride starts and a minimum of 23\text{ ft} at 10 minutes after the ride starts, so the range of heights is \boxed{[23\text{ ft},\ 55\text{ ft}]}. That minimum is also the height of the boarding platform.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} minutes, and so the wheel makes one full revolution every 12 minutes.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of t that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(t-1)=0 \implies t-1=0 \implies t=1

Part (b). The amplitude is A=16, so the quantity rises 16 above the average value and falls 16 below it:

\text{maximum}=59+16=75^\circ\text{F}\qquad\text{minimum}=59-16=43^\circ\text{F}

The warmest month on average is August and the coolest is February, so the range of monthly average temperatures is \boxed{[43^\circ\text{F},\ 75^\circ\text{F}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

Part (a). The midline of a sinusoid d(x)=A\sin[B(x-h)]+D is y=D, and the midline is the average value of the oscillation. Here D=9, so the water averages \boxed{9\text{ ft}} deep.

Part (b). The amplitude is A=4, so the quantity rises 4 above the average value and falls 4 below it:

\text{maximum}=9+4=13\text{ ft}\qquad\text{minimum}=9-4=5\text{ ft}

High tide is at 8:00 a.m., when the depth is 13\text{ ft}, and low tide is at 2:00 p.m., when the depth is 5\text{ ft}, so the range of depths is \boxed{[5\text{ ft},\ 13\text{ ft}]}.

Part (c). Here B=\frac{\pi}{6}, so the period is

\text{Period}=\frac{2\pi}{B}=\frac{2\pi}{\pi/6}=2\pi\cdot\frac{6}{\pi}=12

The period is \boxed{12} hours, and so the water returns to the same depth every 12 hours. High tide therefore occurs twice in a 24-hour day, and low tide twice as well.

Part (d). The phase shift is the value of x that makes the argument of the sine equal to zero:

\frac{\pi}{6}(x-5)=0 \implies x-5=0 \implies x=5

The phase shift is \boxed{5} hours, and so the pattern is shifted 5 hours to the right: at 5:00 a.m. the water is at its average depth and rising. High tide is at 8:00 a.m. and again at 8:00 p.m.; low tide is at 2:00 p.m. and again at 2:00 a.m..

Part (e). Substitute x=12 (noon):

d(12)=4\sin\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(12-5)\right]+9=4\sin\left(\frac{7\pi}{6}\right)+9

=4\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)+9=7

So the model gives exactly \boxed{7.0\text{ ft}} at noon.
